SLIDE 02 / 08ANALYTICAL LENS
The analytical lens

Reading public-space AI through three layers

Floridi et al. (2018) sit behind most of the AI ethics guidance currently in use, including the OECD principles and most institutional codes. The problem, as Mittelstadt (2019) argues, is that principles by themselves do not get enforced and do not translate into shared practice.

So our analytical lens has three layers. The UN SDGs (United Nations, 2015) set the aspiration. Floridi’s five principles run the ethical test. The EU AI Act (European Union, 2024) classifies the risk. The UK has chosen the principles and skipped the rules (DSIT, 2023).

The three London cases that follow are tested against all three layers, covering embedded AI, ethical dilemmas, and threats to sustainable growth.

SLIDE 03 / 08CASE ONE
Case one — TfL contactless

TfL: a fare gate is a data gate

Wembley Central gateline. I tap in with a contactless card 3–5 times a day. Each tap creates a journey record linking time, station, and a tokenised version of my card.

I tap in three to five times a day on a contactless card. That action sits inside roughly 1.6 billion contactless journeys on TfL’s network in 2024 (Copic, 2025), or about 130 million a month. The AI is not in the gateline. It is in the analytics that pull from the tap and from the depersonalised Wi-Fi signal across 260 stations (TfL, 2019), and the open data feeds that power more than 600 apps and contribute up to £130m a year to London’s economy (Deloitte, 2017).

What this case keeps coming back to is consent. The principle that fails is Autonomy: the only opt-out — leaving the network entirely — is unavailable to anyone who depends on the Tube to live, which means meaningful autonomous choice over data exposure does not exist. Boiten (as cited in Fearn, 2019) made the point that telling people to turn off their Wi-Fi is not a real opt-out when the alternative is not using the Tube. The 2024 cyberattack made it harder to argue otherwise. Around 5,000 customers’ bank details and home addresses were accessed in that breach (Scroxton, 2024), and TfL had no way to give them the choice to never have shared that data in the first place.

The analytics layer most likely falls under limited risk with transparency obligations under the EU AI Act, while the linked law-enforcement data feeds raise the higher-tier classification question separately. The UK has no equivalent statutory test for either tier — the classification question simply does not arise.

SLIDE 04 / 08CASE TWO
Case two — Smart parking ANPR

Smart parking: the same camera, two different rulebooks

Empire Way Public Car Park, two minutes from Wembley Stadium. ANPR enforcement icon visible top right of the tariff board. Ordinary day £10. Stadium event day £35. The 3.5x surge runs on the same camera.

I walked past an ANPR enforcement camera at the Empire Way Public Car Park, a private commercial site two minutes from Wembley Stadium. It is mounted on a pole, no taller than a streetlight, and tens of thousands of drivers pass under one daily without noticing.

The camera’s actual customer? The reading goes to two different places. For policing, the read goes into the National ANPR Service, where around 11,000 cameras submit roughly 50 million records every day (NPCC, 2020). For private parking, the same read becomes a Parking Charge Notice. In 2024–25, private operators issued 14.4 million of those, each a £100 contractual claim against a driver who never knowingly signed a contract (RAC, 2025). At Empire Way, the same ANPR runs a £35 event-day surge over the £10 ordinary rate. Justice fails because the £100 PCN and the £35 surge run through a private operator’s internal review process, not statutory appeal — so the driver’s challenge route is procedurally weaker than the operator’s enforcement route.

The plate counts as personal data under UK GDPR (ICO, 2024). The algorithmic decision sitting on top of it does not fall under any UK AI law, and the EU AI Act would not catch it either.

SLIDE 05 / 08CASE THREE
Case three — Brent Council post-Casey CCTV

Wembley: a camera built for a near-miss, watching every Tuesday

Olympic Way, Wembley. Brent Council CCTV mast, part of the post-Casey Zone Ex deployment. The stadium arch is the asset the infrastructure was built to protect.

I stood under a Brent Council CCTV mast on Olympic Way looking up at the stadium arch. The cameras above me exist because of a specific failure. On 11 July 2021 around 6,000 ticketless fans stormed the Euro 2020 Final, and Baroness Casey later called the day a near miss with real risk of fatalities (Casey, 2021). Brent Council, the FA, the Met Police, and the stadium operator built the post-Casey response together: a Zone Ex coordination centre, expanded CCTV across Wembley Park and Wembley Central, and integrated event-day monitoring (Brent Council, 2026).

Beneficence here has a documented case behind it. The justice question is harder to answer. The residents bearing the daily surveillance burden are not the visitors whose disorder generated the rationale. Brent is one of London’s most diverse boroughs, and its residents now carry the surveillance cost of visitor disorder they did not cause.

The cameras currently run crowd analytics rather than biometric identification. Article 5 of the EU AI Act prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement, with narrow exceptions covering imminent threat, missing persons, and suspects in defined serious crime categories. None of those exceptions fit general borough CCTV, which is why adding facial recognition here would trigger the prohibition rather than fall within it.

SLIDE 06 / 08SYNTHESIS
The synthesis

Comparison: one square mile, three rulebooks

Case EU AI Act tier Floridi principle failing UK regulatory gap SDG impact Verdict
TfL contactless Between limited and high; no UK equivalent test Autonomy — no real opt-out from the data trail ICO under UK GDPR SDG 11 mixed (mobility +, breach harm −); SDG 9 + (open data) Public benefit funded by mandatory data exposure
Empire Way ANPR Outside high-risk schedule; algorithm caught by no one Justice — £100 PCNs and £35 event-day surges with no statutory appeal Nobody on the algorithm; ICO on plate data only SDG 16 − (asymmetric appeal); SDG 11 − (commercialised access) Same camera, two rulebooks — the weaker one earns the money
Brent post-Casey CCTV Limited risk today; tier 1 prohibited the moment FR is added Beneficence justified; Justice failing on residents Surveillance Camera Commissioner; ICO if FR added SDG 16 + (real safety case); SDG 11 − (uneven burden) Built for a near-miss, watching every Tuesday
What changes across these three cases is not the camera. It is which rulebook applies. Three cases, the same underlying technology, one square mile — three EU AI Act categories, three different Floridi failures, three different UK regulators (and one gap where no regulator applies), pulling SDG 9, 11, and 16 in different directions.
SLIDE 07 / 08THREATS & OPPORTUNITIES
Threats and opportunities for sustainable growth

The price of being a stadium borough

Wembley Park is one of the UK’s largest regeneration projects and one of London’s most surveilled square miles. Quintain has invested £2.9bn since 2002, the site draws 16.4 million visitors a year, and 6,000 of a planned 8,500 homes are now delivered — the largest single-site build-to-rent neighbourhood in the country (Quintain, 2025). That is real SDG 11 progress: sustainable cities, jobs, public realm.

SDG 16 tells a quieter story. Brent has 338,918 residents, 85% from ethnic minority groups, 31% living below the poverty line, the second-highest BAME share in England and Wales (Trust for London, 2022; ONS, 2021). They host the surveillance infrastructure that makes the stadium economy possible: TfL data flows, ANPR enforcement, post-Casey CCTV. They cannot vote on it.

AI does deliver value here. The question is whether the bargain between SDG 11 and SDG 16 is fair, and who gets to decide.

SLIDE 08 / 08CLOSE
What I take from one square mile

Reflection & recommendations

As a student of AI for business, what surprised me building this journal was that the technology was the easier half to analyse. The rulebook around it was the harder one.
For citizens
A single-page statement at each major data collection point, naming the operator, the algorithm, and the route of redress.
For regulators
Close the algorithmic-decision gap that UK GDPR currently leaves open — the plate is covered, the decision on top of it is not.
For Brent Council
Publish event-day surveillance impact assessments that include ordinary-day coverage, so residents can see the full scope of what operates in their borough.
